title: The Complete Canada Travel Guide
subtitle: Turquoise Rockies lakes, French colonial cities and a wildlife-rich north, spread across the world's second-largest country
summary: How to plan a Canada trip: which region to choose, when to go for the best weather and open roads, what it costs, and a practical twelve-day Western Canada itinerary.

sections.title: How Canada divides
body: Canada divides into distinct regions separated by real distance, not just a line on a map — a first trip realistically covers one.

**Western Canada.** [[vancouver|Vancouver]], [[whistler|Whistler]], [[banff-lake-louise|Banff and Lake Louise]] and [[jasper-national-park|Jasper]] — mountains, glacial lakes and the country's most photographed scenery.

**Central Canada.** [[toronto|Toronto]], [[niagara-falls|Niagara Falls]], [[montreal|Montreal]] and [[quebec-city|Quebec City]] — the country's biggest cities and its French colonial heart, all connected by a manageable train corridor.
**The Maritimes.** [[prince-edward-island|Prince Edward Island]] — a slower, seafood-and-lighthouses side of Canada, distinct from either coast.
**The North.** [[churchill|Churchill]] — polar bears, beluga whales and the northern lights, reached only by plane or a long train ride.
sections.note: Most first-time visitors pick Western Canada's mountains or Central Canada's cities — both work as complete trips on their own and don't require internal flights within the region itself.

list.title: If this is your first trip
list.text: [[vancouver|Vancouver]], [[banff-lake-louise|Banff and Lake Louise]] and [[jasper-national-park|Jasper]], the classic Rockies route.

list.title: If you want walkable historic cities
list.text: [[montreal|Montreal]] and [[quebec-city|Quebec City]], Canada's most European-feeling corner.

list.title: If you're travelling with kids or want an easy city break
list.text: [[toronto|Toronto]] paired with [[niagara-falls|Niagara Falls]], an easy, low-effort combination.

list.title: If you want skiing or mountain adventure
list.text: [[whistler|Whistler]], one of North America's best ski resorts.

list.title: If you want a slower, seafood-focused pace
list.text: [[prince-edward-island|Prince Edward Island]], a world away from the mountain parks.

list.title: If you want a singular wildlife experience
list.text: [[churchill|Churchill]], the polar bear capital of the world.

sections.title: Getting around: flights, driving, and one common mistake
body: Canada's continental scale means flying between regions and driving within them, rather than one mode covering the whole trip.
**Fly between regions, don't drive.** [[vancouver|Vancouver]] to [[toronto|Toronto]] takes over 40 hours by road versus 4.5 hours by air.
**Rent a car for the Rockies.** [[banff-lake-louise|Banff and Lake Louise]] and [[jasper-national-park|Jasper]] have limited public transport between viewpoints and trailheads.
**Use the train corridor in Central Canada.** [[toronto|Toronto]], [[montreal|Montreal]] and [[quebec-city|Quebec City]] are well connected by frequent Via Rail service, no car needed.
**Book Churchill flights well ahead.** [[churchill|Churchill]] has no road access — flights from Winnipeg are the only fast way in.
sections.note: Book flights and Rockies lodging months ahead for a July or August trip — Banff and Jasper's peak season sells out early.

sections.title: When to go
body: Canada's vast range means 'the best time' depends heavily on region, though **June to September** works well almost everywhere.
**Summer** brings the most reliable weather nationwide, with every mountain road and trail open.
**Winter** is superb for skiing in Whistler and Banff, and for aurora and polar bear viewing in Churchill, though many mountain routes close.
**Shoulder seasons (spring and fall)** are workable in the cities, with fall offering excellent colour in the Rockies and Quebec alike.
sections.note: Book Banff, Jasper and Whistler accommodation several months ahead for peak summer or ski season — both sell out their best options early.

list.title: Six days: the Rockies highlights
list.text: [[banff-lake-louise|Banff and Lake Louise]] and [[jasper-national-park|Jasper]], the most popular short Canada itinerary, flying into Calgary.
list.tip: Fly into Calgary rather than Vancouver — it's much closer to the Rockies.

list.title: Twelve days: the classic Western Canada loop
list.text: The itinerary on the [[c:canada|Canada country page]]: [[vancouver|Vancouver]], [[whistler|Whistler]], [[banff-lake-louise|Banff and Lake Louise]] and [[jasper-national-park|Jasper]]. A complete first look at Western Canada.
list.tip: Book Moraine Lake's shuttle or arrive before 6am — the access road often closes to regular cars by mid-morning in peak season.

list.title: A week focused on Central Canada's cities
list.text: [[toronto|Toronto]], [[niagara-falls|Niagara Falls]], [[montreal|Montreal]] and [[quebec-city|Quebec City]], connected by train.
list.tip: No car needed — Via Rail's corridor covers this entire route comfortably.

list.title: A Maritimes or Churchill add-on for a second trip
list.text: [[prince-edward-island|Prince Edward Island]] or [[churchill|Churchill]], the parts of Canada most first-time visitors never see.
list.tip: Book Churchill's polar bear season (October–November) flights and lodges up to a year ahead — capacity is limited.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Canada?
faq.a: Ten to fourteen days covers one region properly, such as the Western Canada loop in this guide. Six days works for a focused Rockies-only trip.

faq.q: Should I fly into Vancouver or Calgary for the Rockies?
faq.a: Calgary sits much closer to Banff and Jasper; Vancouver adds a worthwhile city and the Sea to Sky Highway if you have the extra days.

faq.q: Do you need a car in Canada?
faq.a: Not in Toronto, Montreal or Quebec City, which are well connected by train and transit, but yes for the Rockies and Prince Edward Island.

faq.q: Is one trip enough to see Canada?
faq.a: No, not — the country's regions differ enough that most visitors return for a second, entirely different trip rather than trying to add more to one.
